name: Advanced Refactoring Patterns
description: This module documents advanced, specialized refactoring techniques reserved for unusually complex, large-scale, or non-standard situations — it does not apply to small, typical, everyday refactoring work where the basic approach is already sufficient.
content:
This module documents advanced, specialized refactoring techniques reserved for unusually complex, large-scale, or non-standard situations — it does not apply to small, typical, everyday refactoring work where the basic approach is already sufficient.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Before starting refactoring work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
2. Document any non-obvious refactoring decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
3. Keep refactoring changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
4. Keep refactoring outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
5. Validate refactoring outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
6. When multiple refactoring strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
7. Re-check edge cases relevant to refactoring (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid introducing new refactoring abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of refactoring correctness.
- Do not silently drop refactoring edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid mixing unrelated refactoring concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for refactoring, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
